strengths: Well-motivated framework combining SMC samplers with gradient-based optimization, with clear presentation and comprehensive appendices
Shows existing methods (JALA-EM, Carbone et al. 2024) as special cases, providing valuable unifying perspective
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple settings with fair comparisons (equalized kernel applications) and insightful visualizations of density evolution
Practical contributions including ESS analysis (Propositions 3-5) and adaptive step-size scheme that provide actionable insights
Rigorous treatment of stop-gradient approximations and surrogate losses in appendices, addressing subtle autodiff issues
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: Proposition 2 analyzes only the idealized scheme with exact expectations; convergence for the actual particle-based algorithm (Algorithm 1) is deferred to future work, significantly limiting theoretical impact

Limited theoretical novelty: primarily applies existing SMC theory (Del Moral et al. 2006); Proposition 2 is standard gradient descent analysis; ESS bounds (Props 3-5) are incremental with restrictive assumptions (Gaussianity, bounded Hessians globally, exponential moments)

Computational efficiency claims need scrutiny: SOSMC requires 2 energy evaluations per iteration vs ImpDiff's 1; wall-clock comparisons (Figure 6) show only modest advantages; fresh reward evaluation overhead not fully accounted for

Limited experimental scale and scope: restricted to 2D toy problems and 28×28 MNIST with no high-dimensional experiments; missing comparisons with score-matching methods or other variance reduction techniques; SOSMC failure modes unexplored
Unresolved practical guidance: no formal analysis of how to choose ESS threshold τ, step-size parameter c, or when SOSMC is preferred; adaptive scheme in Remark 4 is ad-hoc; limited ablation studies

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing an important class of applications (MMLE, EBM training, reward tuning) with clear practical relevance
General SMC-based framework that unifies existing methods as special cases, demonstrating breadth and clarifying the design space
Comprehensive experiments with fair comparisons to baselines, particularly strong demonstrations of improved particle reward tracking and faster convergence in multi-modal settings
Solid theoretical analysis including exact gradient recovery (Lemma 1), convergence rates under standard assumptions (Proposition 2), and practical insights on ESS decay (Propositions 3-5)
Mature implementation with careful treatment of subtle issues: stop-gradient quantities, surrogate losses for automatic differentiation, and thorough experimental protocols detailed in appendices
Clear presentation with good motivation, logical flow, and extensive algorithmic/experimental details supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: convergence guarantees (Prop. 2) apply only to idealized scheme with exact expectations; finite-sample convergence of particle-based algorithm is deferred to future work without characterization of approximation error

Computational cost analysis incomplete: SOSMC requires ~2× more gradient evaluations per iteration; experiments show ImpDiff faster in wall-clock time for Langevin setting; costs of weight normalization and ESS bookkeeping not quantified

Limited algorithmic and theoretical novelty: SMC for gradient estimation exists in prior work (SMC-EM, Cuin et al. 2025); main contribution is systematization rather than new techniques; theory mostly applies established SMC and optimization results

Narrow experimental scope focused primarily on EBM reward tuning; missing experiments on MMLE with latent variable models despite being key motivation; only one high-dimensional experiment (MNIST); limited baseline comparisons

Heuristic adaptive step-size scheme (Remark 4) lacks theoretical justification; ESS thresholds appear arbitrary; strong boundedness assumptions in convergence analysis (Propositions 4-5) may not hold in practice; no ablation studies on design choices
